tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Advance a continuous-time signal by shifting each key time point, breakpoint, and support interval T units to the left while preserving the signal's shape and values.

image_slots.image_description: Instructional schematic on a time axis showing a continuous-time signal before and after advancing by $T$. Show the original signal and the advanced copy on the same axes, with the advanced copy shifted left by $T$ units. Include one labeled key time point moving from $t_0$ to $t_0-T$, a clear left-pointing shift arrow, and enough whitespace that the identical shape is obvious.

blocks.text: Advancing a signal means moving the entire waveform left by $T$ units. The rule is simple: subtract $T$ from every time coordinate, but leave the waveform values, widths, and overall shape unchanged.
In the simplest base case, a single labeled feature at $t_0$ moves to $t_0-T$. That is the whole idea of an advance: the feature stays the same, and only its time location changes.
The same left shift applies to every key time point, breakpoint, and endpoint in the graph. If a signal is described by a landmark time, the advanced signal uses the same landmark moved left by $T$.
So an interval $[a,b]$ becomes $[a-T,b-T]$. The important check is that only the time locations change; the amplitudes, widths, and ordering stay the same.

sections.section_title: Moving a Key Time Point Left by an Advance Amount

example_content.example_prompt: Advance a signal with one labeled feature at $t=7$ by $3$ units and identify the new feature time.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is one labeled feature at $t=7$. For an advance, subtract the shift amount from the time coordinate and keep the feature's value unchanged.
So the new feature time is $t=4$. The feature stays the same; only its time position moves left by $3$ units.

sections.section_title: Advancing a Signal Graph Without Changing Its Shape

image_slots.image_description: Instructional graph on one set of time axes showing a continuous-time signal before and after a left shift by $2$ units. The original waveform should include a few distinct landmarks, such as a rise, a peak, and a flat or zero segment, so the translation is obvious. Overlay the advanced waveform on the same axes with identical heights and widths, shifted exactly $2$ units left. Label corresponding landmarks on both copies and include a clear left-pointing arrow labeled $2$.

example_content.example_prompt: Advance the plotted signal left by $2$ units and sketch the result on the same axes.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a full signal graph with several visible landmarks. For an advance, treat the waveform as one rigid shape and move every time location left by $2$ units.

Mark each endpoint, peak, corner, and flat region on the original graph. Then subtract $2$ from each time coordinate: a feature at $t=a$ moves to $t=a-2$, and a segment from $a$ to $b$ moves to $[a-2,b-2]$.
Now redraw the same heights and widths at the shifted times. The advanced graph keeps the same shape, the same values, and the same relative order of features; only the horizontal position changes.

example_content.example_prompt: A finite-duration signal is nonzero on $[1,6]$ with breakpoints at $t=2$ and $t=4$. Advance it by $3$ units and identify the new breakpoint times and support interval.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-duration signal described by its support interval and interior breakpoints. For an advance, subtract the same shift from every endpoint and breakpoint, then keep the piece order unchanged.

So the new support interval is $[-2,3]$, and the new breakpoints are $t=-1$ and $t=1$. The original three subintervals $[1,2]$, $[2,4]$, and $[4,6]$ become $[-2,-1]$, $[-1,1]$, and $[1,3]$ after the shift.
That is the whole move: every boundary moves left by $3$, and the signal remains zero outside the shifted support interval.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Advance Amount from an Original and Advanced Signal

image_slots.image_description: Instructional comparison on aligned time axes showing the same continuous-time signal before and after a left shift. Include the original signal and the advanced signal on the same plot, with one clearly labeled landmark moving from $t=5$ to $t=3$ and a matching support boundary moving from $t=1$ to $t=-1$. Use a clear left-pointing shift arrow labeled $2$ to make the advance amount easy to read.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the original and advanced signal plots to determine the advance amount $T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a pair of aligned plots showing the same waveform before and after a shift. To find $T$, match one visible landmark on the original signal with the same landmark on the advanced signal and read the leftward time difference.
The peak moves from $t=5$ to $t=3$, so the leftward shift is $5-3=2$ units. That gives the advance amount directly.
Check the support boundary too: $t=1$ moves to $t=-1$, which is the same $2$-unit difference. The advance amount is $T=2$, and the direction stays explicit: the signal moved left.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Advance a continuous-time signal by shifting each key time point, breakpoint, and support interval T units to the left while preserving the signal's shape and values.

sections.section_title: Moving a Key Time Point Left by an Advance Amount

prompt_blocks.text: If a feature at $t_0=9$ is advanced by $T=4$, which time is the new feature location?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Advance means subtract the shift amount from the original time: $9-4=5$. The feature moves left to $t=5$ and its value stays the same.

prompt_blocks.text: If a feature at $t_0=\frac{11}{2}$ is advanced by $T=\frac{3}{2}$, which time is the new feature location?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Advance means subtract the shift amount from the original time: $\frac{11}{2}-\frac{3}{2}=\frac{8}{2}=4$. The feature moves left to $t=4$ and keeps the same value.

prompt_blocks.text: The plot shows the original signal and a left shift of $T=2$. Which choice shows the advanced signal without changing its shape?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The correct graph is the whole waveform translated left by $2$ units. Every landmark moves left by $2$, so the support changes from $[-1,3]$ to $[-3,1]$, and the heights and widths stay the same.
The other choices either shift right, leave the graph unchanged, move by the wrong amount, or change a height instead of preserving the rigid shape.

prompt_blocks.text: The plot shows the original signal and a left shift of $T=3$. Which choice shows the advanced signal without changing its shape?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The correct graph is the whole waveform translated left by $3$ units. Every breakpoint moves left by $3$, so the support changes from $[-2,2]$ to $[-5,-1]$, and the shape stays unchanged.
The other choices either shift right, leave the original graph in place, move by the wrong amount, or alter a height instead of preserving the rigid translation.

prompt_blocks.text: A finite-duration signal is nonzero on $[2,9]$ with breakpoints at $t=4$ and $t=7$. Advance it by $2$ units. Which shifted breakpoint/support-interval list is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Support interval $[4,11]$ with breakpoints at $t=6$ and $t=9$.
Support interval $[0,7]$ with breakpoints at $t=2$ and $t=5$.
Support interval $[0,7]$ with breakpoints at $t=4$ and $t=7$.
Support interval $[0,9]$ with breakpoints at $t=2$ and $t=5$.
Support interval $[1,8]$ with breakpoints at $t=3$ and $t=6$.

questions.correct_answer: Support interval $[0,7]$ with breakpoints at $t=2$ and $t=5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Advance by subtracting $2$ from every endpoint and breakpoint. So $[2,9]$ becomes $[0,7]$, and the breakpoints move from $t=4,7$ to $t=2,5$.

prompt_blocks.text: A finite-duration signal is nonzero on $[1,10]$ with breakpoints at $t=3$, $t=5$, and $t=8$. Advance it by $4$ units. Which shifted breakpoint/support-interval list is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Support interval $[5,14]$ with breakpoints at $t=7$, $t=9$, and $t=12$.
Support interval $[-3,6]$ with breakpoints at $t=-1$, $t=1$, and $t=4$.
Support interval $[-3,10]$ with breakpoints at $t=-1$, $t=1$, and $t=4$.
Support interval $[-2,6]$ with breakpoints at $t=0$, $t=2$, and $t=5$.
Support interval $[-3,6]$ with breakpoints at $t=3$, $t=5$, and $t=8$.

questions.correct_answer: Support interval $[-3,6]$ with breakpoints at $t=-1$, $t=1$, and $t=4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Advance by subtracting $4$ from every boundary. So $[1,10]$ becomes $[-3,6]$, and the breakpoints move from $t=3,5,8$ to $t=-1,1,4$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Advance Amount from an Original and Advanced Signal

image_slots.image_description: Two aligned continuous-time signal plots on shared time axes showing the same waveform before and after a left shift. The original signal has a single clear peak at $t=5 and support from t=1 to t=7$. The advanced signal has the same shape shifted left, with the peak at $t=3 and support from t=-1 to t=5$. Highlight the matching peak and the left support boundary. Include a left-pointing shift arrow with no number label.

Two aligned continuous-time signal plots on shared time axes showing the same waveform before and after a left shift. The original signal has a flat-topped plateau from $t=4 to t=6 and support from t=2 to t=8$. The advanced signal has the same plateau from $t=0 to t=2 and support from t=-2 to t=4$. Highlight the leading edge of the plateau and the left support boundary. Include a left-pointing shift arrow with no number label.

prompt_blocks.text: The plots show the original signal and its advanced version on aligned axes. What advance amount $T$ produced the shift?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the same visible landmark in both plots. The peak moves from $t=5$ to $t=3$, so the signal shifted left by 2 units.
The left support boundary also moves from $t=1$ to $t=-1$, which confirms the same advance amount.

prompt_blocks.text: The plots show the original signal and its advanced version on aligned axes. What advance amount $T$ produced the shift?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the same landmark on both plots. The plateau edge moves from $t=4$ to $t=0$, so the leftward shift is 4 units.
The support boundary also moves from $t=2$ to $t=-2$, which confirms the same advance amount.
